summary: Intro to Redwood Optimize console: walk through batching, prefix/KV cache recommendations, run cost model scenarios for Ravenwood's low-latency search assistant. Agreement to run a 2-week sandbox pilot and share security pack + pricing sheet.
topics: Ravenwood production profile and latency targets
Cost model scenarios and sensitivity to TTL and sessionization
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, um i'll kick off. good to meet the ravenwood team. quick agenda—console tour, econ scenarios, then q+a.
[00:18] Priya Shah: hey thanks alex, glad to be here, we want to see concrete numbers — our SLAs are 120ms median for interactive search sessions.
[00:34] Jamie Ortiz: great, that's tight but doable depending on model variant and sessionization, we'll show tradeoffs. mi— mike, can you remind us of your average query length and sessions per user?
[00:48] Mike Chen: yeah average prompt is ~38 tokens in, about 120 tokens out, sessionized so same user may have 4-6 turns within a session. throughput spikes are around 1.2k rps at peak.
[01:04] Nina Valdez: thanks—so we focused the demo on two levers: prefix/KV cache (lookahead prefetch) and adaptive batching in the runtime. we'll load the ravenwood profile into the console.
[01:20] [screen share noise, brief silence]
[01:38] Jamie Ortiz: okay showing the Optimize console, top-left is workload profile import. we preloaded ravenwood's sample trace you shared. first slide => baseline (hosted small-v2 model) cost per 1M tokens: baseline $42k/mo (note: numbers illustrative).
[01:58] Priya Shah: that seems high—what's driving most of that?
[02:03] Jamie Ortiz: mainly per-token for generation + low batching due to strict latency target. but with session KV and prefetch we can convert many repeated prefixes to cache hits and increase effective batch sizes.
[02:20] Mike Chen: can you explain prefetch vs session cache? our infra folks use 'sessionization' already but not sure implementation details.
[02:30] Alex Park: quick bucket: session cache keeps KV per session in memory (fast, high hit for repeated contexts). Prefetch/lookahead proactively primes KV on next-turn candidates (trade extra compute when client pattern is predictable). sometimes prefetch is called 'look-ahead' and we see 15-30% incremental hit-rate depending on UX.
[02:50] Sara Li: and what's the memory impact of KV per user? we can't keep huge state for millions of users.
[02:58] Jamie Ortiz: good call — console suggests a TTL policy per session and a size budget; for Ravenwood's 1.2k peak rps with average session length we recommended a tiered TTL: 2 min active, 20 min soft for warm users, with eviction LRU. that gave a 42% effective hit-rate in our sim with 60GB KV working set — numbers in the scenario panel.
[03:26] [typing sound]
[03:34] Alex Park: now i'll flip the cost model: scenario A = no cache, 120ms SLO, batch size forced low => cost X. scenario B = session-only cache with 40% hit => cost drops ~34%. scenario C = session+prefetch (predicted 20% additional hits) => cost drop ~48% but note slight median latency increase for some cold requests.
[03:58] Priya Shah: what's the risk of hallucination or output variance if we reuse cached KV?
[04:06] Jamie Ortiz: cache is KV state of model activations, it doesn't change model weights. output variance can occur if you prefetch a wrong future prefix — but we recommend conservative prefetch policies with confidence thresholds and model variant fallback. console has a simulation slider to tune aggressiveness.
[04:24] Mike Chen: show the math for how hit-rate influences cost — i want to present this to finance.
[04:31] Nina Valdez: sure, go to the 'Savings breakdown' tab — here's tokens saved, GPU utilization gain, and the net monthly cost. you can export a csv. for your profile, 1% absolute increase in hit-rate roughly equals ~0.8% cost reduction under our baseline assumptions.
[04:52] [screen flicker]
[05:00] Jamie Ortiz: now batching: we demo a dynamic-batching policy tied to latency windows. if you allow a 20ms batch window we can get average batch sizes of 6-8 tokens which lowers per-token amortized scheduling. the console sim shows throughput vs p99 latency curves.
[05:22] Priya Shah: 20ms sounds risky for UX — users may feel lag. can we target only non-interactive flows?
[05:29] Alex Park: absolutely — route by policy. Redwood routing can send high-priority low-latency users to warm dedicated capacity and route bulk requests through batched paths. that's a core differentiation.
[05:42] Mike Chen: how do we model dedicated vs hosted cost in the console? Evan — sorry, nina, show the 'Dedicated' pane.
[05:49] Nina Valdez: yeah dedicated amortizes instance cost; console calculates breakeven point — for Ravenwood, monthly steady-state >$X (redacted in recording) you break even on a 3-node dedicated pool versus hosted. we included burst patterns and can simulate partial reserved capacity.
[06:10] [participant cough]
[06:15] Sara Li: security: SOC2, KMS: we need encryption of KV at rest and audit logs. what's supported?
[06:22] Alex Park: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs, the security pack we'll share lists SOC2 attestations, SSO/SAML, RBAC policy examples. for KV encryption we recommend server-side encryption with customer keys in Private or Dedicated. hosted offers envelope encryption.
[06:40] Priya Shah: okay good. what about data residency? we have EU regs for a subset of users.
[06:45] Jamie Ortiz: we can route EU traffic to EU regions and pin model variants & caches there; console policy routing supports region tenancy.
[06:54] Mike Chen: timeline — if we start a pilot, how long to run meaningful bench?
[06:58] Alex Park: the team recommends two weeks for the sandbox with real traffic replay or an A/B targeting of 5-10% of traffic to collect hit-rate and latency signals. that gives statistically significant delta for cost and quality.
[07:14] Daniel Ortiz: what about instrumentation? we need token-level cost breakdown in our dashboards.
[07:19] Nina Valdez: Console outputs a token-level CSV and we can hook the tracing hooks to your datadog/newrelic. also has per-route cost and per-model traces.
[07:30] Priya Shah: any competitor we should be aware of from a procurement perspective?
[07:34] Alex Park: customers often compare with CloudAI endpoints and ModelServeX — CloudAI is simple but less prescriptive on batching/caching, ModelServeX has strong on-prem options but less runtime batching sophistication.
[07:48] Mike Chen: could you run a sensitivity: what if TTL is 5x longer — memory goes up but hit-rate increases, is there a diminishing return?
[07:57] Jamie Ortiz: yep — here's the sensitivity chart, hit-rate improves with TTL but plateaus; beyond 4x TTL memory costs dominate; prefetch can be more cost-efficient than brute TTL increase for your pattern.
[08:12] [short pause]
[08:18] Alex Park: quick demo of console's optimizer: click 'Suggest' — it proposes a mix: session TTL 3m active, prefetch confidence .65, batch window 12ms for low-latency routes, longer 40ms for bulk. Also suggests quantized model variant for background queries.
[08:38] Priya Shah: quantized model — any quality regression? we're sensitive to recall.
[08:43] Jamie Ortiz: small regression in rare cases, the console ties eval sets to campaigns — you can pin a conservative variant for high-RRR queries and let background flows use quantized models.
[08:56] Mike Chen: okay that helps. can you also share the scenario assumptions so finance sees the line-by-line?
[09:02] Nina Valdez: yes we'll export the assumptions + csv; also include a short write-up on where the uncertainties lie (prefetch accuracy, session churn).
[09:12] [overlap chatter]
[09:20] Daniel Ortiz: procurement: price model for pilot? do we get a discount?
[09:24] Alex Park: pilots often have sandbox credits; for enterprise pilots we do a limited-time discounted reserved pricing if you commit to an evaluation contract—we'll follow up with formal pricing.
[09:35] Priya Shah: last question: can we run a live benchmark in your sandbox? we want end-to-end numbers with our replay.
[09:42] Jamie Ortiz: yes we'll provision a sandbox cluster and help replay your trace. recommended footprint for your trace is 3x production burst capacity to capture tail.
[09:52] Alex Park: okay wrapping up — recap and next steps in a moment. any other burning things?
[09:57] [silence]
[10:02] Alex Park: recap: 1) We'll provision 2-week sandbox for Ravenwood with replay of your trace; 2) Share security pack, SOC2 docs, and KMS config examples; 3) Export cost model CSV and assumptions for finance; 4) Schedule a deep-dive with SRE on KV sizing and eviction policies.
[10:22] Priya Shah: that works for us. thanks all.
[10:27] Mike Chen: thanks—excited to see the replay results.
[10:31] Alex Park: thanks everyone, we'll send calendar invites for the follow-ups.
[10:36] [meeting ends]
